utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. The Chamber has allowed the accused to make a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis today during the first session. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, everyone. Today I will be addressing you as the accused, not as a self-represented defendant as before. I am a physician, a psychiatrist, psychotherapist, group analyst, and a literary man. Instead of being accused for the events in our civil war, I should have been rewarded for all the good things I've done; namely, that I did everything in human power to avoid the war; that I succeeded in reducing the suffering of all civilians; that the number of victims in our war was three to four times less than the numbers reported in the public; that I proclaimed numerous unilateral cease-fires and military containment and I stopped our army many times when they were close to victory; that I constantly sought peace and accepted four out of five peace agreements; that I advocated, initiated, and implemented the humanisation of the conflict by applying all measures of humanitarian nature; that in addition to my many presidential duties, I personally supervised a supply of humanitarian aid, cease-fires, and the honouring of international law of warfare, and thus I was the address for many successes of humanitarian actions; also, I proclaimed and implemented many acts of mercy. As time passes, this truth will be stronger and stronger and the accusations and the propaganda, the lies and hatred, will get weaker and weaker. I never had anything against Muslims or Croats; on the contrary, I became a Sarajevo man of my own choice. I arrived in Sarajevo when I was 15, although all my countrymen went to Belgrade, and although in Belgrade I had my father's sister and other family. I chose Sarajevo of my own will. I got married there. My wife Ljiljana and my children Sonia and Aleksandar were born there. I was friends with the people of Sarajevo, making no distinctions, and I was friends with them deeply and sincerely. All my colleagues in psychiatry, my friends, my dentists, my tradesmen, my lawyers, all of them were Muslims. I never made any discrimination. My hairdresser of many years, Meho Sabic, is a man I visited a few days before the war started, hoping that there would never be a war, and I was always faithful to my choices. I never allowed for the possibility of even the smallest individual crimes, and especially not crimes on a mass scale, nor the possibility that any of the communities would be permanently removed from the Serb territories. Neither I nor anyone I know could ever think there could be a genocide against any people that we believed to be the same as us, Serbs, although of a different confession. My other occupation is literature. I authored several books of poetry, including one of poetry for children. These books have been awarded by many prominent awards and my poems have been translated into several great languages. After leaving my presidential duties, I also wrote one comedy and one novel called: "The Wondrous Chronicle of the Night." I was active in politics until 1968 -- from 1968, in fact, and after that for decades I was a dissident, and beginning with 1990 until 1996 I was also active as a founder and the president of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also as a member of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then I was president of Republika Srpska. My wife and I were also active in a political movement led by a prominent Muslim woman. If it hadn't been for the creation of political parties, I would still be in that movement today because I was otherwise not interested in politics. I was born on 19 June 1945 in a village called Petnijca, not far from Savnik in present-day Montenegro. Until the Berlin Congress, it was Herzegovina, and that's why we felt so close to Bosnia-Herzegovina because we thought of ourselves as Herzegovinians. My father was a tradesman. My mother was a housewife. My family on my father's side had monarchistic sympathies, whereas my mother was more on Tito's side. My father was active in the so-called Liberation Movement when the war started, but then the communists killed off the prominent elders in our family, those are the well-known leftist inclinations. And at that time my father chose the royalist army which was later suppressed by Tito. And then my father came home. My father was very fond of Russian [as interpreted] culture and Russian [as interpreted] monarchy and parliamentarianism. When -- after 1968 I stopped believing Tito, I was then 32. I was then 23, in fact. I came to see the rightness of my father's views, and until then we argued a lot. I see in the transcript that he was fond of Russian culture, in fact it was British culture and parliamentarianism. In that army, the royalist army which was referred to as Chetniks, these Chetniks in my area did not have any conflict with other ethnic communities. They only had an idealogical conflict with communists. In Montenegro in my region in Niksic, there are Muslims who live there, even very close to my home and they were very close also to my parents and our family. The Muslims of Niksic are very renowned people, very prominent athletes, physicians, et cetera, and there had never been any interethnic conflict or any bad sentiment between communities. The Catholic church was very close to my school and there I came to love Bach listening to the organ music. Therefore, my experience with the so-called others were more than good and favourable, and my father had a friend as close as a brother who was a Muslim, who was an Albanian. And I never had any bad experience of that sort, and that's why I chose to live in Sarajevo. In the 1990s, the Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 became very anxious when the HDZ appeared in Croatia and when the Izetbegovic made his announcement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serbs were frightened of the Ustasha rhetoric and there were also suspicions that Mr. Izetbegovic, the author of the Islamic Declaration, would apply this Islamic Declaration as a political platform of his party. There is not a single Serb or any man anywhere in the world who could convince Serbs that there is or isn't a threat of genocide. It is only when they saw where things were going in Yugoslavia that they understood what's the writing on the wall before I even said a word. The Serb party was established only after those two other political parties, the HDZ and the SDA, had been founded already with their very strong anti-Serb political orientation. I was neighbours with Mr. Izetbegovic. We met very often and my literary friends defended him in the former regime. They did not agree with the Islamic Declaration, but they didn't think that he should be in prison either. I often queried him about what his party was going to be like and I had the most favourable impression of him, and I told my friends that this man could not possibly do anything that is written in the Islamic Declaration. And when it became clear that the Serb party had to be established, I informed Mr. Izetbegovic, but he already knew that from a certain Mr. Srebrovac, who had been in jail with him. And when I said that Srebrovo and myself would be together, he was kind of down-cast. I don't know why. But he seemed glad that the Serbs would also have their own political party. He asked me that the Serbs should not vote for communists among their community because it was customary for people in one community to vote for the worst people in the other community. So he asked me that Serbs should not vote for Muslim communists. Mr. Izetbegovic was very concerned that the communists would remain in power and that he and his group would perhaps end up in jail for the third or fourth time. I agreed and we did not vote in the way he feared. We voted honourably. And my agreement with Mr. Izetbegovic was that if we win, at the next elections every community could vote from any of the four ethnic lists; and that still applies in the Federation, one voter can vote either from the Croatian and Muslim list. And if it had been so, there would be no problem. Mrs. Plavsic received many votes from Muslim women; we were able to see that. Quite simply, those Muslim women were happy to see a woman on the Presidency and we saw a light at the end of the tunnel, a possibility to live well together. However, despite all the resistance that I felt I had to become part of the Presidency, although I had been refusing to be nominated to the parliament or the Presidency, and I said that after the elections I would return to my profession which is physician first and author next and I would not be politically active. I'm afraid the interpretation is not correct. I refused to be nominated and I did not become member of the Presidency or the parliament. My determination was to remain physician and author. Everybody who knows me know that I am not an autocrat, that I am not aggressive, that I am not intolerant. On the contrary, I'm a mild man, a tolerant man with a great capacity to understand others. But it is true that I was strict towards myself and others in implementing democratic decisions. I did not abuse the great powers given me by the status in the party or the great parties given me later by the Constitution in Republika Srpska. Immediately after the elections, tensions rose in Bosnia-Herzegovina and our pre-electoral ideal was ruined because the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, which represented the Muslim community, changed its main orientation in favour of Yugoslavia. Already in the end of January, in mid-January we established the authorities and in end January the SDA chose secession. In establishing the authorities, the Serb side, the SDS and myself, made many concessions to keep peace in the house. In numbers we were almost equal to Muslims if we take Serbs who declared themselves as Yugoslavs; however, Croats and Muslims got the most prominent posts. The Muslims got the post of president of Presidency, a Croat became the prime minister, and the Serbs had to satisfy themselves with getting speaker in the Assembly. However, there were also ministries of power, the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence were given to Croats and Muslims. Even the foreign ministry came under the control of a Muslim, namely a man whom we knew would take Bosnia in the direction of fundamentalist regimes instead of the direction of Europe. Then came a period of underhand dealings and blockages in establishing the authorities. The Serbs could not get the posts that they were promised. A Serb could not become the head of MUP. Marginalisation started. A period of peace time, underhand dealings, and trickery, and we could live with all that still but we were very concerned about manipulations with the MUP. The MUP became one with the Party of Democratic Action. The SDA sent its members for military training in Croatia with the intention that these people upon return be integrated into the MUP and into that army of the republic that was in the making already on the 30th of March. On the 10th of June, the National Council for the Defence of Muslims was already established. Some people who were convicted were also included in this, people who had been convicted many times before and all of that presented a great danger to us. What the Serbs had lived through in areas where there were less than 50 per cent, such as Visegrad for instance, for the entire year not a single community in Europe would put up with that, with the humiliation, even rapes, even murders. If I tell you that on his patron saint's day a Serb would invite a Muslim and play good host, you know what the patron saint's day means for a Serb, and after that the same man kills him on the door-step of his own home, it is not individual pathology. This man obviously thought that it could be done, that was the case with the killing of the member of the wedding party on the 1st of March, 1992. The father of the groom was killed and some other people were killed, but this was not done by one of those Celos. He said it on television. He said that that goes nowadays. In every municipality, in every area where we lived together, the military organising of Croats and Muslims was no secret to anyone. We could see it, it was obvious. Arming and the similar problems, when I discussed that with Mr. Izetbegovic, what was happening among the people, he would simply shrug his shoulders and say, "Well, everybody's arming themselves." It was clear we were heading towards a catastrophe. We simply made political movements. We were relying on the Constitution, on the local self-government, and we were aiming for regionalisation. Mr. Izetbegovic - of whom I still think positively because I believe that he was pushed into the war - he suggested to us at the end of May 1992 to split Bosnia. We were shocked. He gave that proposal to Mr. Zulfikarpasic as well, he did it at least twice, and Mr. Zulfikarpasic wrote about that. We clearly stated we were against the division of Yugoslavia, against the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the Croats accepted the idea, and then somebody came up with an idea to exchange populations. We branded that a nightmare and rejected that idea as well. Following that, the Zagreb daily Vecernji List published an idea of cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mrs. Plavsic on behalf of the Serb community stated that it was an interesting idea, letting them know that we did not reject outright such peaceful suggestions. So all of the political movements we made at the time were made in, so to speak, dire straights, when we were pushed into a corner. We were pushed into a corner by the movements of our partners in government and by our neighbours of other ethnic communities and we were forced to do that. Those were the things we had to do from the founding of the party until the war broke out and until the end of the war. Throughout that time our reactions and my personal reactions were aimed at minimising the damage and doing what we had to do under the circumstances. The president of the Muslim-Bosnian organisation, the second Muslim party, Mr. Zulfikarpasic, one day in the summer of 1992 called me on the phone. I was about to go on a trip when he told me that we had to get together to save Bosnia and conclude historical Muslim-Serb agreement. I cancelled all of my other engagements and gladly accepted to meet with him, gladly expected the idea presented to me, and it seemed to me at the time that Mr. Izetbegovic also genuinely accepted that idea. We were expected to give up on the idea of regionalisation and to keep Bosnia in itself entirety in Yugoslavia. Upon return from America, Mr. Izetbegovic discontinued his further support to that project. And starting in the end of August there was an increase in tensions. And it was only then that we founded the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was done by the local population and nobody could really take it against them because there were several Muslim municipalities being established at the time, and the people in that region did not want to accept the domination of Sarajevo, and neither did they want to accept the domination of Pale throughout the war. They really wanted to have a sort of local self-government which they wanted to ensure for themselves. Mr. Izetbegovic once came back from Germany and he looked quite beaten and discouraged, and he said to me and Mr. Koljevic that he was being pushed into fighting for independence and that he had no other choice. Those were really, really difficult moments, and at the time it really seemed as though somebody was pushing him to fight for the independence. Throughout that period, even though we could observe that the Muslims and the Croats were organising themselves in the military sense, the entire Serb elite, the intellectuals, members of the party, the leadership of the party, were against the SDS establishing a paramilitary formation. And the SDS never really had one. In all of the foreign intelligence services, there was speculations to the effect that perhaps Captain Dragan was a member of the SDS, but they could never claim with certainty that that was the SDS paramilitary formation. I myself and the entire Serbian political leadership didn't really know what attitude the JNA would take. At the time the JNA had an identical attitude towards national parties. It was an ideological conflict, if I can call it that, and we had a great dilemma as to what to do should the war broke out. Our young men were serving in the JNA, whereas their young men were under their control and under their command. So during that time I was faced with a lot of pressure from the ground. Local authorities were quite concerned - justifiably concerned - because they felt abandoned by the federal government, they felt abandoned by their own leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were left to themselves to resolve a multitude of big and small problems. So in turn, they pressured us. The only means they had at their disposal that nobody could take away from them was the Territorial Defence, which according to the law belonged to each local commune. And everybody not only could but had to under the law defend their country once it was attacked. There was no way to betray that people, nor could I have accepted something that they would not have accepted themselves because it would have lasted for a very short time, only two hours. This is the nation that had a long memory, that remembered everything that had happened to them in the past, and there was no way one could dictate to the Serbs what they should be doing. So we had enormous pressure exerted on us because the people were afraid that they would all be massacred, and during that time the Serbs were being killed. It is a terrible misconception and it is a great injustice, this portrayal of the Serbs as those who started the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbs were exposed to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina even before the 4th and 6th of April. A member of the wedding party was killed on the 1st of March, and then there were -- on the 25th and 26th of March there was a terrible massacre in Brod and then in Sijekovac. On the 5th of April, or rather, on the 4th of April already in Sarajevo, the Green Berets attacked the barracks, Serb communities, and they occupied all tall buildings, skyscrapers, put their snipers there, they killed policemen, they killed young people who tried to cross into Grbavica which was already under Serb control. So that was a night of terrible terror in Sarajevo. So the beginning of fighting and the beginning of the war in various municipalities have nothing to do with me. At the time when these killings were committed in Brod, Bijeljina, Kupres, we still had the common state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Simovic and others, Mr. Ostojic, they went to those hot spots on a task given by joint authorities to calm the situation. They were not sent there by the SDS. Simovic was on our list, but he was not a member of the SDS. These people were tasked by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had among its members some Serbs, as there were Serbs in the Presidency and people were sent on these tasks as representatives of the common joint government. On the 1st of March, 1992, a member of the Serb party was killed in Sarajevo the day after the referendum. Mr. Koljevic and I were in Belgrade at the time, so we were not responsible for the barricades. The barricades were a spontaneous, a chaotic reaction to the possibility that somebody could dare to kill a Serb in front of an Orthodox church, that somebody could dare shoot at the wedding party without there being any protection for that wedding party. We had no influence over the joint police. The police was controlled by the Muslims, by the Muslim SDA, by their extremists. And before our very eyes it was transforming itself into the illegal army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We ourselves were completely powerless. My escorts who were policemen in the joint MUP escorted my family in the 11th hour on the 5th of April outside of Sarajevo under fire. I was still myself in the Holiday Inn hotel in Sarajevo, and from there together with two other national leaders I went to the TV station where we had -- we were guests in a live TV show. We were trying to give our views to the audience. In front of that time -- at that time there were 50.000 protesters in front of Holiday Inn. Some of them were armed, and this is why my escorts did not allow me to go back to the hotel even though I wanted to do that. However, two of my body-guards remained there. They ended up being taken prisoner, mistreated, they barely managed to stay alive. We were also very concerned for the fate of Professor Buha, however it seemed that some smart people managed to get him outside before that enraged crowd broke into the hotel and started firing. So the only issue that I should be put on trial for is the social and political stupidity which came as a result of excessive trust that I had in people, and we and the Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina could have paid a very high price for this stupidity of mine. The first manifestation of war was the expulsion of Serbs from the towns where Croats and Muslims were in majority. In the parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Serbs were a minority, they were fair game, perfect targets, and they never took to arms to defend themselves. And until September 1992 there was not a single Serb settlement in the Muslim and Croat Federation that was left intact. Everything had been cleansed, killed, set on fire. Quite to the contrary, in Republika Srpska in the -- in what is today Republika Srpska and at the time was part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where we were in majority, there were no traces of war there at the time. Your Excellencies, there was no pattern of behaviour in the Serb municipalities. If we look at the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Sarajevo and in the predominantly Muslim areas, we see that it was raging starting on the 5th of April, whereas in the neighbouring Serb Rogatica the war didn't start until the 20th of May. So it is clear that in the areas that were under Serb control there was no war. The Serb side didn't start a war and no war was started until the Muslims initiated it. Most of the municipalities in Republika Srpska saw war at the end of May, those were the municipalities of Bratunac and Vlasenica, which already had reached an agreement on creating two municipalities and having a peaceful coexistence there. Mrs. Rabija Subakovic, an eminent Muslim, wrote an open letter to Izetbegovic asking him to support this sort of a project. In other municipalities as well. And instead of supporting her, an order came out ordering the Muslims in Bratunac and Vlasenica to start shooting, and those two municipalities were turned into a slaughter-house, and it was not the result of any will of mine, I did not know about this. This came as a result of negotiations and the attack of arrogant extremists from the SDA party. This is how it was in the Krajina municipalities also, where despite the fact that there was a war in other Bosnian municipalities, no war broke out in Krajina municipalities until it was initiated by the extremists. Until that time they had their own police, they had their own co-operation, and life was going on similar to how it is regulated nowadays in the European Union. And the co-operation ended at the end of May at the order of the SDA, which we could hear from one witness. Based on their strategic interest, to ensure that the left bank of the Sana River were annexed to Cazin and Bihac. So they started from the Sana River and its left bank. I didn't know anything about that. I learned about all that only later. We did not have any reliable communication lines with Krajina for a few months, not only because there was no corridor or the corridor was broken off. The corridor was actually stabilised towards the end of the year, but that was not the only reason. Another reason was the fact that we didn't have even telephone lines. The valley of the Sana is comprised of Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Bosanski Novi. Those four municipalities were torched towards the end of May and the beginning of June, and that was all based on the strategic interest which was for that area on the left bank of the Sana River to be annexed to the Cazin Krajina. Although we did not have any communication lines over there, we didn't have any contacts there, the Autonomous Region of Krajina had its parliament, its government, its ministers, they tried hard. The Krajina people had always been of autonomous views. The Serbs want to be autonomous wherever they are. We had our reliable people over there; for example, the president of the Assembly Mr. Kupresanin, on my behalf and on his own behalf toured in Vega -- remand prisons, he helped the prisoners there, he co-operated with the UNHCR, the International Red Cross, the local Red Cross. He alarmed the general public about the possible peril that threatens the civilians. He went to Manjaca, he went to the prison in Prijedor. He wanted to help. He wanted to diminish the sufferings. However, there were no prisons anywhere before Prijedor came under attack. The prison was an investigative centre because the remand unit or the detention unit could only hold up to ten people, not more. And then on the 30th of May there was a large-scale attack on Prijedor which resulted in the arrest of a large number of people. 59 per cent of those people were released immediately after the triage process was completed. Those prisons were not camps. Those prisoned existed only for as long as the investigative judges were there and the investigators, and they worked every day, they worked hard. As soon as all the investigative actions and the triage were over, 41 per cent of the people were sent to Manjaca because they had participated in fighting and some were also subject to criminal proceedings and the rest were released. In other words, there were no prisons before the war, before the clashes, and there were no clashes before the end of May. However, we didn't know even that, we didn't have any insight, we didn't have any way to learn about all that or make our mark. Srdjo Srdic from Prijedor, he was the president of the Red Cross in -- at Prijedor, also an MP. Whenever he could, he informed us what was going on, what was happening. He tried hard to inform us, and he gave me firm guarantees that there was no barbed wire around Trnopolje, but I could only see that for myself subsequently. At that time I was in London, at the conference there. I personally invited a British journalist to come. I spoke to Penny Marshall and her team and I even transported them on our government's aircraft. I opened Republika Srpska for them. I told them they could visit anything that they wanted to see. I encouraged them to take escorts where they wanted. If they didn't want, they didn't have to take escorts. I didn't want to hide anything. That was my first motive. And the second underlying cause was to have the presence of the journalists to curb the influence of some of the renegade elements amongst us. That was another one of my stupidities because there is no country in the world who would let the journalists to the front line. But I can tell you that the journalists who introduced themselves as journalists to us did a lot more damage to us than NATO's shells. For example, they would stage a scene where a man would be put next to the barbed wire, although he was not there previously, and then they took a picture of that and sent off that image to the world. Thomas Deichmann exposed that and now it is very clear; however, at that time this was -- this could not be denied. Every reader had seen that. So you could not go to every reader to explain that things were not what they seemed. We continued to attend conferences to discuss Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of our moves at that time were reactions to the Muslim's side moves. It was only on the 16th of April that we set up our own Territorial Defence because the Muslims had expelled us from their own Territorial Defence and they removed a Serb general. On the 22nd of April, I launched a platform and I suggested that nothing that had been taken by force should be recognised because any further fighting from that would have been pointless. And all that time we participated in the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina under the -- chairmanship of Lord Cutileiro and Lord Carrington and then the chairs became Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen. That was the continuation of that same conference. However, the war raged against our will. There was no way to influence the events. We took the decision on the setting up of our army on the 12th of May, but it was only on the 15th of June that we actually organised it or made a decision on its organisation. We spent the entire year of 1992 in trying to structure the Army of Republika Srpska, and we went into great pains to turn common people into soldiers, and they fought only in the territory of Republika Srpska. And it was defence, all the time we defended ourselves. We never embarked on trying to conquer Muslim territories because it was abundantly clear that there would be a division, i.e., the reorganisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three different republics and we had under our control over 60 per cent. So I knew that it would be crazy to take even more territory that we would eventually have to give back. This put us into a very difficult situation where we had to passively defend ourselves, we suffered a lot of casualties, especially during the so-called truces when we suffered more losses than at the time when we were actively engaged in fighting. The events in the municipalities followed a certain logic. Apart from Foca and Zvornik, everywhere else - and of course Bratunac - were already -- at the beginning of May Zekic was killed, but that was four weeks after the 8th of May, after the war had broke out in Zvornik. So apart from Zvornik and Foca, and we did not know anything about these two, in all the other municipalities war broke out much later. In Zvornik, we didn't know what was going on there, we didn't have a clue. Nobody ever invited Arkan there. I don't think that he was ever there. Maybe some of his men were there. There were a lot of paramilitaries there. However, on the 16th of April, our police didn't know who was in control of Zvornik and our police, the secretary from the ministry called Arkan on the phone and asked him who was in control of Zvornik. The same applied to Foca. The late Mr. Koljevic went there with Jeremy Braden [phoen] in April to assist, to see what was going on with the Serbs who were left at the elements' mercy and they almost killed them there. So that had nothing whatsoever to do with us. We could not influence any of those events. Now that I have mentioned my participation in conferences, Your Excellencies, many events, many incidents happened while I was abroad attending negotiations or meetings. I knew that things were not happening was because I was not there, but because those incidents were staged during the conferences in order for the conferences to fall through. On the 20th of May, there was an explosion in Vase Miskin street. It is no longer in my indictment but it is a very significant model. The ambassador Cutileiro called me on phone and he told me that he had to interrupt the conference, we were in Lisbon at the time, because a shell, a mortar shell, had killed people in a bread line. I took an hour's break in order to inquire with our army and the police as to what had happened and they told me it was a nonsense. They told me we did not fire any shells. It was impossible to fire a shell in such a narrow street. They told me that the media had already been there prepared to film an event, and then I was very certain that we didn't do it and I told Mr. Cutileiro that and that he shouldn't buy that rubbish. That was a model that was followed when the other incidents in Sarajevo happened. Unfortunately there were also crimes. For example, Koricanske Stijene, which was not staged my Muslims, it was done -- it was committed by criminals. And I was also at a conference at that time. The army informed the state leadership, they informed me, I was shocked, I was angry, and I asked that the two presidents of the municipalities shed some light on the crime, to take measures. I shouted at some innocent people, especially the leadership of Skender Vakuf which is today's Knezevo. We ended the conference on the 27th of August. On the 28th I flew to Belgrade. On the 29th I was in Pale. And on the 30th Minister Subotic was dispatched to the spot of the crime. (redacted

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: At the end of September 1992, Muslims from Srebrenica killed a lot of civilians and soldiers between Srebrenica and Milici, and in Vlasenica there was a mass burial. Also as -- on my way to next round of negotiations I stopped by and I attended the burial and I delivered a sad and humble speech which we had an occasion to hear in the this courtroom. It was a terrible scene. Between Srebrenica and Vlasenica and Bratunac and Zvornik, we were in a large room. There were about 20.000 armed Muslims there. We sent them messages that they shouldn't fight, that that area would be given to Muslims. However, we suffered losses. Workers were being killed, farmers in their fields, miners in the mines, they were all being killed. And we used all the round-about ways across Sekovici and Sapardici [phoen]. But they would come even there. They would set up ambushes, they would kill civilians, they would stop buses and kill all the civilians there. They prevented us from having any sort of communication, and they rendered impossible the survival of Republika Srpska and the people in that area. For an entire year up to the spring of 1993 we suffered all that, we didn't do anything, but then we had to launch a counter-offensive in order to neutralise them. Then we took Cerska, Konjevic Polje, and so on and so forth, and it was then that we saw an unprecedented campaign about blood flowing in Cerska, about a huge number of people having been killed, although what we found there was houses torched and Serbs crucified after having been kidnapped. We found all sorts of things there. However, this story about the Serb crimes in Cerska was just a cry wolf and one couldn't match that in the international media. If General Morillon had not gone there to inspect the situation, the story would have held and it would go down in history as a genocide that had been committed by the Serbs. And then the families went to Tuzla, whereas the able-bodied men went to Srebrenica. It was their choice. They went to Srebrenica to fight there. We continued with our activities, we proceeded with our actions. I stopped our army. Some of my generals understood that. Some were very angry. Common soldiers, foot soldiers, were very angry when I stopped our army at the very entrance into Srebrenica in 1993 because I knew up to then that 1300 Serbs, mostly civilians, had been killed, and the soldiers were from those families, the families that had been killed. And the Ministry of Defence from some more big countries published their communiques, saying that we had entered Srebrenica and that there were again flows of blood on the street. That candidate of lies and propaganda about the crimes that had been committed is similar to what happened after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995. The rhetorics was the same, the way things were represented were the same. And again, it was another cry wolf situation, but nobody could believe that. Your Excellencies, I trust the international community. I often came at odds with our army. I attacked our officers for having done things which they didn't do, as a matter of fact. It turned out that I tended to believe rumours more than my own officers, and they were in dire straits. They were between a rock and a hard place, and so was I because I tended to accuse them, attack them, because I believed the allegations and most of them were simply not correct. One of the most common such misunderstandings, or rather, the sources of misunderstandings between the civilian authorities and the army was the issue of convoys. I had thousands of other concerns and worries. I had almost 2.000 kilometres of front line and if I -- although I was not engaged in technical command, I was still concerned with the supplies for the army, the food supplied to them, people who lived along the front line and how they lived. However, despite of all that and despite of my engagement in the negotiations with the international community, I found time every time somebody asked me to help with the passage of a convoy. We have heard - and I assure you - that at any given moment there were about 700 trucks on the roads of Republika Srpska. There were times when Croats stopped humanitarian aid for Muslims and the only way sometimes for the humanitarian aid to reach Muslims was through Serb territory. However, there were many problems with the convoys. The problems arose due to the great number of trucks or goods that had not been declared or because these transports appeared at check-points where they had not been announced and the soldiers there did not know anything of these convoys, and still in all those situations we did our utmost so that civilians on the other end of the line would get the aid. This kind of assistance is a tradition that Serbs introduced from the Serb-Bulgarian war and Henry Dunant, the founder of the International Red Cross, was aware of that. Every time aid came for poor people in Bulgaria, the Serbs stopped the fighting to let the aid through. Professor Koljevic, one of the greatest humanitarians and one of the best men I have ever known, was made ill by all his efforts to get the convoys through. And in those contexts too I often accused unfairly our local commanders because the Muslims, together with the humanitarian aid, received all the military equipment they needed. After every humanitarian convoy we suffered many more losses because they received weapons, ammunition, and fuel along with the aid. And I had terrible difficulties trying to neutralise the rage of our people who saw for themselves that it was not humanitarian aid, it was military equipment. And despite my busy schedule, it never happened that I was too busy to respond to any invitation, any suggestion, that we tried to alleviate the situation and the suffering. Let's take Sarajevo. We were almost 200.000 in Sarajevo before we were expelled and between 50- and 70.000 Serbs remained in Sarajevo; they were not allowed to leave. Sarajevo is my city. And any story that we would shell Sarajevo without any reason is absolutely untrue. Every shell that fell on Sarajevo hurt me personally. That was a city where I knew every square foot, but that city had over 2.000 legitimate military targets and I proposed that Sarajevo be demilitarised. That was rejected. I suggested that it be placed under UN administration; that was rejected. They wanted and they managed to keep Sarajevo militarised to the maximum with 50- to 70.000 troops inside, three divisions, one inside the city and two around the city, and they managed to ruin every cease-fire and to create incidents to feed the media, at the same time demonising Serbs, and keeping alive the hope of the Muslim leadership that somebody from the international community would get sucked into the war, involved in it, on their side. Examples of this are incidents in Sarajevo. Mass killings and the suffering of people, including women and children, in lines for water and especially Markale I and II. It is shameless propaganda and tricks that produced the desired result during the war, but it is unimaginable that this is appearing now in the courtroom and that the Court is verifying it as real events. The first incident, Markale I, was staged after the 4th of February, when this attempt to orchestrate an incident with the humanitarian aid queue failed and already some days later in February at an empty market-place where there are no goods on sale, 500, 600 people are suddenly there and this massacre is staged. I always asked our army to keep me informed, and you will see it in all the documents. I always said, "Please admit to it if it's our work. It will do less damage if we admit it because we have to be credible. If we say something it has to be true." And the army convinced me that it was not possible to hit such a place with one shell, there was no visual contact, and it was impossible. It was not even believable that 500, 600 people would be in such a small space - they had no reason to be there. And it was, on top of everything, impossible to create such damage in view of all the stalls and tables. It is a shameless orchestration. Obviously some people got killed by that explosion, but we also saw android mannequins being thrown onto trucks creating this show for the world. We resolutely rejected that and we said that we would not accept any investigation unless the Serb side is somehow involved in it. The investigation was completed without us and we were not allowed to do our own investigation. Now, as for Markale II, Markale II was orchestrated in an attempt to take the crisis to its peak in May, and that attempt failed. And the strategic bombing that was supposed to change the balance of powers and to make us sign a surrender also failed. However, another opportunity was taken in end August 1995 by this orchestrated event known as Markale II. Our side could not have fired that shell nor could that shell hit that spot in that way. However, again we were not allowed to take part in the investigation. Some investigating authorities from the international community co-operated with the Muslim police and harmonised their findings, although they should not have done that. So we were in a situation when there was nobody unbiased there who would be able to say what was actually going on. Muslims enjoyed such support in this trickery but we were helpless. We could just stand by and watch this catastrophe in the making without being able to do anything. Markale II is a glaring example. Again, there was an explosion there. Some people were killed. But there were also bodies there that had never been on the market before the explosion. Some were brought from the front line and also some bodies of people who had died of natural causes were brought from the morgue and added to the number of casualties. All of this was done to create this image of catastrophe and suffering. Now, speaking of sniping, I was always horrified by sniping because I believe it to be inhumane, although it is a legitimate military technique of eliminating important personalities on the side of the adversary. We in Sarajevo were not able to distinguish by appearance who were Serb, who were Muslim; we are of the same race and there was no reason to engage in any intense sniping activity. I myself worked on many anti-sniping agreements, some of which were signed, but not many were implemented, not many were honoured. Along the front line in the city of Sarajevo itself, Muslims were in a more favourable position in terms of range than us. They had positions on top of the highest buildings. They hit and sniped wherever they liked. They killed our young girls and women. They also shot people. And they employed champions in marksmanship to do this. Incidents around the Vrbanja bridge they presented as Serb activities, although that was automatic fire that went on all day. They engaged in this kind of trickery and crime that could be exposed only by a totally unbiased, impartial observer group, but that was sadly missing because all members of the international community there came with enormous prejudice against the Serbs and there was no way for us to get our truth across, to make it see the light of day. We were completely trapped. Nothing that we did around Sarajevo was ever accepted. We never cut off any water, electricity, or gas. It was they who fired at the transformer station and cut off water, but they never had any shortages of water. They only had shortages of power. Water was in our hands. They sold water on the black market and those who were engaged in this trade simply did not want water to be available free of charge. Concerning modified air bombs, I heard very vaguely that they are being researched, that they are being fitted with engines from some rockets, and that they were being tested at the grounds of the Army of Yugoslavia to make new firing tables for them. Nobody was required to ask me for permission for any innovations or modifications in the army and nobody asked me. But this is another aspect of command, the military technical aspect into which I never interfered -- with which I never interfered. But I never heard that such a bomb was ever used in a populated area. I heard it was used to crush bunkers in mountains or perhaps somewhere in the military industry, but not that it was ever used in a populated area. There was never any piece of news believable to any degree about that. As for Srebrenica 1995, I was not involved in tactical and operative command or control, but whenever I passed through a place where there was some sort of command, especially a corps command, I stopped by to greet those people. And that's how I stopped by Vlasenica before the operation in Srebrenica, sometime on the 25th, the 26th of June, and by that time we were several days into the horrific Muslim offensive around Sarajevo and Naser Oric's forces stretched our forces thin and co-operated with the forces in Srebrenica. I need not remind you what this protected area looked like. It was a military ground for excursions of Naser Oric's forces who avoided conflict with the VRS. They terrorised civilians. They gouged their eyes out and tore off their ears, only to come back to the safety of the protected area after that. I gave my approval to a small-scale operation to separate Srebrenica and Zepa, to narrow it down to the urban core, as agreed. And that operation was supposed to separate and cut off this corridor between Srebrenica and Zepa that was used for the transport of military equipment and weapons. On the 9th, on the morning of the 9th, the Muslims decided not to defend Srebrenica and the local leadership asked Sarajevo to let them surrender Srebrenica and let the population evacuate. The same day General Krstic asked for instructions because he was able to enter Srebrenica and he wanted the opinion of the superiors. I gave our approval. By that time I had stopped our army many times. Our army was called stop-and-go. We did not want to win; they wanted to win. They wanted to have all of Bosnia for Croats and Muslims. We did not want that kind of victory. We didn't want all of Bosnia for ourselves and that's why we were not in favour of war, war was not in our interest. I gave approval to enter Srebrenica. The only civilians we expected to find in Srebrenica were Muslims. There was not a single Serb there. I ordered that these Muslims be protected, that all the facilities be protected, I ordered that a police force be established immediately to protect civilians. I knew that some of the refugees would probably want to go elsewhere, but it never crossed my mind that the entire population would want to leave Srebrenica; to us it came as a complete surprise. Ambassador Akashi told me that the place was packed, that they were not allowed to leave, that they were not allowed to leave, but it was because their leadership didn't let them leave. It was not us. We did not receive any information about mistreatment of civilians. I did not receive any information of even individual murders in Srebrenica. I got reports of high tensions in Bratunac, where there were a lot of prisoners and very few troops because Bratunac Brigade was outside of Bratunac. And elderly military conscripts and young boys were guarding a lot of prisoners. It was not the only time when we had a lot of prisoners. There were many situations during the war when we had prisoners under our control. It was the usual procedure: Capture, triage, and separation of those who were not subject to prosecution and who are sent to exchanges and the others who were subject to prosecution. We sometimes effected exchanges directly on the front line or we would send prisoners, the second group, to camps such as in Batkovic or prisons and then on they would be exchanged. Never once during the war was there any situation where we would interfere in a normal situation where prisoners were treated normally, and as soon as they reached Batkovic or another prison they were available to the International Red Cross and everything was all right. Those were neighbours taking each other prisoners and there were sometimes exchanges even before they ever reached Manjaca or Batkovic. Personal contacts were used to organise these exchanges immediately, and the usual procedure was to send prisoners to Batkovic and then organise large-scale exchanges. Very frequently I showed -- I pardoned numerous such individuals and the rest were intended for exchange. They were never subject to any criminal prosecution. There was no indication that anybody was killed in Srebrenica or after that. I never once received any piece of information concerning that, be it verbal or in writing. Those were the same types of rumours that we experienced in 1993 in relation to Cerska and later on in relation to Srebrenica, and one did not need to trust that or to verify that because I would have once again come into conflict with the army, having accused it groundlessly for the umpteenth time. When Mrs. Albright came across a body on a surface, on a flat surface, I ordered that it be investigated. I went on the 22nd or the 23rd of March to the Main Staff and I told the Main Staff that we should not put up with that propaganda any longer and that the Presidency and I myself would order that the most detailed investigation of every single death in and around Srebrenica be investigated. Nobody from the Main Staff opposed that idea. Everybody agreed with me and accepted it. And after that I issued an order to the army, to the police, to the military prosecutor, and everybody else concerned to investigate every single death in and around Srebrenica. Unfortunately, in mid-May, that is to say five weeks later, I transferred my authorities to Mrs. Plavsic and I could no longer follow the situation concerning those events. At the same time, in addition to those existing 2.000 kilometres of front, I was given an addition in the mileage with the addition of the front in Western Slavonia. There were numerous municipalities falling one after one, Bosansko Grahovo, Glamoc, Drvar, and Bosanski Petrovac were at risk which were almost entirely Serb municipalities, also Mrkonjic Grad with a dominant Serb majority, and there was no reason or anything else to raise the flag indicating that something else had happened. What we saw were the fireworks, were the rumours that we had witnessed back in 1993. So at the time there was no information about it. I did not learn about it until I came here, where I learned about things that happened. Your Excellencies, the Serb local authorities are the model of caring authorities. Nobody was ever armed in those municipalities until there was an attack. The Serbs always offered that there be two parallel structures of authorities, that everybody take care of their own people until there was a final solution. Why would you want to expel somebody if you gave them a premises to have their own police, to have their own municipality authorities in a building right next to you? It never occurred to us to do that. Nor did we want to recognise any fait accompli. We expected that there would be final negotiations at the end. On the 24th and the 25th of January, 1992, I said in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina: If we continue down this road, we will have a religious and ethnical war. The Serbs will go to Serb municipalities, the Croats to theirs, the Muslims to theirs. There would be mass murder, there would be blood flowing, and in the end we will have to sign an agreement and have three homogenous ethnic communities, and this is exactly what happened. I offered that we wait with holding a referendum, to wait for the government to be restructured, Cengic accepted that, and the Serbs were supposed to go to the referendum and to legitimatise it. We were in an impossible situation. I personally was in an impossible situation, because I was exposing my community to danger because of the concessions that I gave to the other side, because of my peace-loving policies. There was no such example of any other side going to war under so much pressure, faced with so many lies under -- against enemy who was much stronger. In Bosnia and Herzegovina the mobilisation ratio was 2:1 in favour of Muslims and Croats. And once the NATO and everybody else got involved, the ratio was even much, much worse. There is no such example anywhere in the world of that and nobody ever thought of saying: Let us hear the other side. Gentlemen, the truth is on our side and it will only grow stronger. We did everything in our power to avoid the war and to minimise the consequences and the damages. There is no statute of limitations that will run out on that and lies are subject to statute of limitations and we will live to see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Andrey Demurenko is a retired -- [In English] Sorry, I do it in English. Andrey Demurenko is a retired colonel in the Russian army. In January 1995 he joined the UNPROFOR mission in Sarajevo and served there until December 1995 as Chief of Staff for the Sarajevo sector. Colonel Demurenko participated in investigating the shelling of the Markale market on 28th of August, 1995. He went to sites -- to the sites two hours after the shelling. Upon arriving there he observed a crater of the impact. He saw that the experts were there working at the site. Following that, he gave instructions to the UNPROFOR members working at the site and then went back to the headquarters in order to prepare appropriate orders. Upon his return to the headquarters, he learned that the spokesperson of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina had quickly organised a press conference. The spokesman said that this was just another example of an atrocity and a crime committed by Serbian army and that they need to be punished and condemned as the enemies of humanity. There were absolutely no grounds for the spokesman to state something like that because the investigation was not concluded. Colonel Demurenko believed that the UN spokesman did -- what the UN spokesman did was an act of provocation. Colonel Demurenko received two reports that day. The first one was the report made by a Dutch officer who was a ballistics trajectory expert. The second report was produced by a ballistics expert who was either a Croat or a Bosniak. They established the angle of approach of descent at the time the shell reached the surface. It was a very important document which allowed Colonel Demurenko and his team to proceed with the investigation. Colonel Demurenko gathered a group of experts. Their first task was to make ballistics calculation in order to either confirm or deny the information given by the first expert on the angle of impact of the shell upon the surface. Second, to calculate the angle of the shell and draw the line of descent on the map. Further, the investigation was supposed to include personal inspection of all possible fire positions of that particular shell, including photo documentation of those locations. They worked for three days on 28th, 30th, and 31st of August. On 1st of September, they had the results of investigation together with appropriate conclusions. When he came with the results to the investigation -- of the investigation and showed the conclusion to the assistant of the commander and the assistant realised that their conclusions differed from those prepared for the public by the UNPROFOR spokesman, Colonel Demurenko was told: There will be no publishing of your report. It will be impossible to publish it, announce it, or to give this report to the commander. The result of Colonel Demurenko's investigation indicated that the Serbs would not have fired the shell in that incident. Colonel Demurenko visited all possible firing locations of the Serb side and concluded that those locations were either not suitable for mortar use or that there were no traces of mortar. Neither of the locations visited on the Serb side of the confrontation line nor the terrain encompassed with the possible mortar margins of deviation radius that he saw with his own eyes were occupied by mortars on 28th of August, 1995. In other words, the terrain was either not suitable for the use of mortars or the location was not used because otherwise he or his team would have seen the traces of the mortar firing or mortar positions since 120-millimetre mortars are very heavy and leave traces and impressions in the ground. The terrain east of the direction of his investigation, east of 170 degrees plus/minus 5, was rocky and full of slopes, therefore not suitable for the mortars. This would apply to all bearings less than 170 degrees. Colonel Demurenko also concluded that there was a one in million chance that the shell would hit the Markale Market from the distance where Serb positions were located, bearing in mind the size of the street between the building at Markale and the distance from the Serb positions. At that point in time, Colonel Demurenko believed that he had two choices regarding the conclusions of the -- his investigation. The first avenue was to cease any activity and not to do anything else to promote the investigation and truth. Second avenue was not quite appropriate when from the point of view of military ethics and subordination, but he had to resort to it. Through the liaison officer for public relations he got in touch with a media company in order to publicise the report. Colonel Demurenko had been waiting a long time for somebody from the UNPROFOR, from the Sarajevo sector, from the BH command, UN command, for the UN in general to ask him while he was still in Sarajevo: Colonel, could you produce documents to confirm or to corroborate the information that you gave to the Associated Press. But nobody uttered a word about it. Instead, he heard from them only two things: We will throw you out or we will kill you. That was the only argument. Nobody asked a thing. It was undesirable information for everyone. Colonel Demurenko was rejected as a source of information leading in an unwanted direction. It was apparent to him that no one from the UNPROFOR command wanted the truth. Having publicly declared the findings of his investigation, Colonel Demurenko was threatened by Captain Salajdzic, liaison officer between the BH command and the Sector Sarajevo, who told him you have one day of life to live, Colonel. You have no chance of leaving the headquarters. At any intersection you can be killed. An order was issued to kill you. Colonel Demurenko suspected that the attack on Markale II was a terrorist attack from within the city, although a shell can explode only by being fired from a mortar. And if one throws it from the roof, it will not explode. To simulate an explosion of a shell using a different explosive device, however, is not difficult because the crater is the same. Taking the shell and fixing it using screws or whatever else and exploding it with a different detonator will make the crater look the same. These are the factors that make Colonel Demurenko believe that it could not have been a mortar shell. Colonel Demurenko believes that other UN members, such as Lieutenant Colonel Konings, instead of conducting an investigation professionally, focused their information on proving that the Serb side was to blame than rather than simply establish the facts and objective conclusions based on those facts. The UNMOs and the Bosnian police had meetings where they agreed about the method that should be employed in the investigation of the incidents about the type of the projectile, the direction from which it had been fired, and other facts. Colonel Demurenko believed that this was unacceptable and unusual. The UNMOs should have worked independently and in an unbiased manner. One of the main conclusions of the UNPROFOR documents was that a mortar fired from a middle to long range would have a lower trajectory accurate to a firing position in the Serb territory. A lower trajectory round would have passed under the Cymbaline radar's beam. Colonel Demurenko believes this was the wrong basis to conclude that the Serbs fired the mortar shell at Markale II. According to Colonel Demurenko, mortars fired from middle to long range would have had a higher trajectory, not lower, and consequently would not have passed under the Cymbaline radar's beam. Colonel Demurenko believes that the conclusion made in this document was unprofessional and amateur and against the law of physics in the case of mortar fire. This conclusion was made by a G2 officer, a position which was always held by the US army intelligence officer. Colonel Demurenko believes that mass media, journalists, reporters, and his Western colleagues from the UNPROFOR and UNMO were spreading rumours that the Serbs were aggressors and that they wanted to destroy the whole of Bosnia. This idea was unrealistic when he compared it to the situation in the field. Some 60 per cent of the UNPROFOR personnel supported the idea that the Serbs were aggressors because they were presented by their commanders and media with only selected facts, but they were not shown what the other Bosnian Muslim side was doing. The remaining 40 per cent of the UN personnel had their own opinion, but kept quiet about it and only privately dared to express their own different opinion. This correct opinion was always expressed in UNPROFOR reports that tended to blame the Serbs for the situation in Sarajevo. Colonel Demurenko observed that although the UNMO and UNPROFOR were two different forces in Sarajevo with two different chains of command, in practice they were the same people. The task of the UNMO observers was that they were supposed to differ from different types of fire and weapons and to recognise all types of military activities, whether it was an offensive or defensive activity. Many UNMO observers were partial to the Bosnian Muslim side and they informed only about the incoming fire but not about the outgoing fire by the Bosnian Muslims, thereby portraying the fighting in Sarajevo as a Serb aggression and shelling. Colonel Demurenko met twice with the CNN journalist Christiane Amanpour at the Holiday Inn hotel, and he asked her why she always propogated against the Serbs, and she told him that it wasn't his business. Many times those in UNPROFOR had the impression that the Bosnian Muslims were sniping their own population, but it was difficult to prove this because the higher command told them that they should stop this kind of investigation. Colonel Demurenko was aware that the Bosnian Muslim army in Sarajevo was sniping and shelling own civilians. On 8th of June, 1995, Colonel Demurenko released a report stating that the Bosnian civilian was wounded by sniping from a position near the BH parliament which was held by the Bosnian Muslim army. On 30th of July, 1995, Colonel Demurenko released another report stating that Bosnian Muslim forces from the Presidency area were sniping Muslim civilians in Skenderija. On 7th August 1995, Colonel Demurenko released a report stating that mortar shells were fired from Bosnian Muslim positions towards the Skenderija area, which was also in the Bosnian Muslim part of the city. Colonel Demurenko was all ready for war when he arrived in Sarajevo, but there was just occasional exchange of fire and most often by drunk soldiers firing into the sky tracer bullets and so on. He also saw a lot of couples walking in the street which surprised him. It was clear to him that Sarajevo was under the blockade by the Serb forces but also that within the town there were AB -- army -- BH army Muslim -- Bosnian Muslim troops. The Serb troops around Sarajevo were also encircled by the Bosnian Muslim troops from the outer ring. It was also clear to him that the VRS did not want to destroy either the town or the population in the town or even enemy troops, although there was a clear possibility to do so. Colonel Demurenko believes that the Serb forces around Sarajevo did not want to terrorise the civilian population in Sarajevo under the Muslim control. There were 250.000 Serb civilians in the city and the Serb soldiers could not identify the nationality of people by sight. On the other hand, there were individual cases where Serb soldiers who lost their family members acted aggressively. He is 100 per cent sure that the Bosnian Muslim soldiers were sniping and shelling Serb civilians. He went to the Serb side of the city. The life in the Serb side of Sarajevo was exactly the same as in the Muslim part of city. There were problems with food, water, likewise he also -- he was also 100 per cent sure that the humanitarian aid to the Muslim side was ending at the black markets in Sarajevo. This is why they tried to organise direct delivery to the humanitarian aid to the civilians. Colonel Demurenko was aware of BH army offensives from Sarajevo to deblock the city. The biggest part of BH army units was located in civilian buildings. They had some 20 tanks, five to six mortar batteries, either battery some five to six mortars 92 -- 82 and the 120-millimetres, heavy machine-gunners, and so on -- guns, and so on. He saw that the BH army units provoked the Serb forces to respond by opening fire and then moving to other locations. The only incident between the Serb forces and the UNPROFOR in Sarajevo after the NATO bombing of the Serb positions that Colonel Demurenko remembers was the fighting at the brotherhood and unity bridge in Sarajevo. There were two check-points from both Serb and Muslim sides of the bridge and the Serbs and Muslims were shooting against each other. The Serb soldiers then went to an offensive and captured the Bosnian Muslim trenches. The Bosnian Muslims informed the French UNPROFOR about this and the French commander ordered its French troops to attack the Serb unit at the occupied check-point. The French soldiers attacked the Serbs and both French and Serb soldiers got killed in this attack. Both the Serb army and the UNPROFOR took each other's soldiers as prisoners of war. It is obvious that in this case the BH army started the offensive, that the Serbs responded and were bombed, which was unjust and partial action by the so-called impartial third countries. As a result, the Serbs took those UNPROFOR soldiers from the countries that participated in the bombing as prisoners of war. It was a critical point of the war, at which point the Muslim side got the help from the bombing countries. So it was an adequate response from the Bosnian Serbs to respond in this way. The term "hostages" is unacceptable in this situation. The word "hostages" were put between inverted commas because the term "hostage" is not a proper term. Colonel Demurenko did not use the term "prisoners of war" because formally the UN was impartial in accordance with the Geneva Convention and he could not therefore use the term "prisoners of war" for the detained UNPROFOR troops. There was no proper term for the situation so the UNPROFOR used the term "hostages." On 30th of May, 1995, General Smith wrote a message stating that the Serb soldiers captured the UNPROFOR are de facto prisoners of war, that they were captured by French forces in a fight, and that he had ordered command of Sector Sarajevo to hold and secure them. For Colonel Demurenko, it is clear that General Smith and General Gobillard showed their involvement in the war when they actively supported the Bosnian Muslim side. They did not have the right to write this information in the letter, but it was an emotional outburst of General Smith who showed his real intentions. Also various national units within the UNPROFOR fought together with the Bosnian Muslims against the Bosnian Serbs. In June 1995 as a result of a BH army attack, a Russian observation post was occupied. On that occasion the Bosnian Muslim troops took 12 Russian UN soldiers and a Russian lieutenant as a prisoner, but the Russian troops had been ordered not to shoot against any side but they also had the instruction not to let any side use their weapons. As soon as the Russian lieutenant understood that the APC could fall in the Bosnian Muslim hands, he blew it up with a hand-grenade and destroyed the engine of the APC. However, the Russian soldiers were captured and he got information that they would be killed by the Bosnian Muslims. Colonel Demurenko told his French commander that they should organise immediate negotiations because he could not go to the area without the Muslim -- Bosnian Muslims' permission because they would shoot him as well. The general called the Bosnian minister of defence who arranged the permission for him to go and to collect the bodies of his dead soldiers. As the Muslims put it, he ran on foot through the minefield to get his soldiers and told them to follow in his foot steps back to the other side and then to the PTT building, thus casualties were avoided on this occasion. Approximately once a week or once in two weeks UNHCR people were held by BH troops because BH needed the resources, for example, say 200 litres of gasoline. So they detained them and released them upon the delivery of fuel it was, for example. They will stop the UNHCR convoy and ask for the materials the BH would need. If the UN people refused to give, the BH would detain them and take the materials anyway. Pursuant to an agreement between the sides and the UNPROFOR, the city of Sarajevo was supposed to be a demilitarised zone, free of weapons, but that was the case only in theory. Sarajevo under the Bosniaks 'control was full of weapons. Both the military people and so-called civilians had weapons. The notion of uniform was vague, and only for the reasons of not killing each other by friendly fire, the BH people were wearing ribbons, belts, or other signs to recognise each other. Serbian civilians suffered in the Muslim part of Sarajevo. Serbs -- Serb males -- male civilians tried to hide or escape because they were subject to imprisonment and camps. The information about the camps for Serbs was kept away from the UNPROFOR by Bosnian Muslim authorities. UNPROFOR heard about the camps from different sources including Sarajevo citizens. Colonel Demurenko took up a position at NATO headquarters in Mons, Belgium, in 1995 and retired from the Russian army in 1997.
