And he declined to protest against this publicly under pressure of his own superiors. And he refused to have body-guards, which was very strange to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I also noted a reference to the -- to Mr. Petrovic, whom you also refer to in your amalgamated statement. Do you recall that you're referring to Mr. Petrovic also in this article and identifying when it was that you first met him?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I have to admit that I don't remember all of the details and all of the interviews and the meetings I had with thousands of officers and soldiers at the time. I remember that there was a Major Petrovic battalion commander who was placed not far from Grbavica close to the PTT building where the headquarters of the peacekeeping forces was. It would be difficult for me to say anything more than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If this refreshes your memory, you had referred and referred earlier today, in fact, or I think it was referred to in the summary that was read, about retrieving your men by running through the minefield and I believe you explained in the article that you first encountered Petrovic who saw you running through that path and that you then made contact with him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, the mike is working now. I apologise. I have memories which are different somewhat. The most vivid moment of the war for me, given that I had to save 12 soldiers, was when I had to run across a minefield. However, I could not have met Petrovic there. This must have been either a mistake in your information or in the interpretation I received. Petrovic was further away from the place where I was saving the soldiers. I was going back towards the area where the first trenches of the Bosnian battalion were. The first UNPROFOR soldiers that I came across were either from Slovenia or from Slovakia who were very pleased - just like our soldiers were - to be freed and to avoid death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. I also wanted to ask you one question about your expertise in artillery and mortars, particularly in relation to the men you commanded. As I understood your amalgamated witness statement - and indeed what you said in the video that we saw - you -- your expertise developed as a general army commander whose responsibility it was to command subordinate units and know enough about the weapons and the weapons systems that they specialised in in order to do so. Is that basically correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I presume that's also why when you began the effort to investigate into the shelling that you discussed earlier, you gathered specialists and experts in those fields; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. I invited specialists in artillery systems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Colonel, then I'd like to turn to some of the elements of what you discussed briefly today and what was discussed more extensively in the video and obviously in great detail in your amalgamated witness statement. First of all, you explained on the video that you followed a line of direction, a bearing of 176 degrees from Markale; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I used the material -- I relied on the material which had been recommended up until that time by the experts. I relied on the material that initially looked reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the - as we'll discuss a bit later - the particular locations of potential firing that you went to were based then on the angle of descent of the mortar, checked against the number of charges in the firing cable; is that basically right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I will once again try to explain to the best of my abilities. A mortar is a very peculiar kind of a weapon because it is basically a tube without grooves --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't -- I want to give you a full opportunity to explain the things that you need to to answer the questions, but it really will be much more efficient if we move through step by step rather than pausing at various junctures for more elaborate explanations. So I just wanted to indicate the difference between the line of direction which you've just discussed and the particular potential firing points that you identified in the video, which were based on the angle of descent and the number of possible charges. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, there are three factors. There are only six standard charges in mortar rounds, and based on the ballistics expertise discussing 70 degrees of angle of descent - I could be wrong but I think this is not disputed - and 170 degrees southward of the shelling. So the investigation focused on those factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you just say 170 degrees? That's what the transcript indicates. You were previously talking about 176 degrees.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I looked at the documents a number of times. I listened to the comments or to the translation and the figures 170 and 176 were frequently confused, interchanged. And I would like to underline that it doesn't really matter whether it's 170 or 176 because in my interview I said that a margin of error of 5, plus/minus 5, is quite normal. So it could be 175, 165. So that's the first thing. The second thing is when I gave a task to my officer to establish where the firing points could have been, I explored a much broader belt than the one applying to 170 or 176 degrees. I basically photographed all of the slopes on that mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, we're going to talk in a moment about the areas that you indicated during your previous testimony and during the course of the video that you explored, and we'll also discuss that photographs. But for the moment I want to take it step by step and talk about your identification of line of direction. And so do I understand you to say that in your view it didn't matter and you didn't care whether you chose a line of direction of 176 or 165 or anything else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Precisely so, because the reconnaissance of the ground was conducted on a much broader area than the one shown on the sketch. The entire area to the right and to the left, much greater than 5 degrees, was explored so that we wouldn't later be accused of not being thorough enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's -- I want to look at what you said at the time and what you represented that you were doing on the particular day that you -- day or days you conducted your examination of the area. It may well be that the fact that you now say it didn't matter what line of direction you chose affected your consistency in identifying those factors, but I want to check that consistency first. So you -- to begin with, you testified or that is your amalgamated witness statement states at paragraph 122 that UNPROFOR found that the line of direction was 171 plus or minus 5. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Well, I think that's close to the truth. Yes, it sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well at any point you're welcome to check your statement if you --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I take you at your word. I believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we noted before, on the video it says you followed the line of direction of 176 degrees. So that means, Colonel, that you took one of the extremes of the margin of deviation and used that as your line of direction rather than the line of direction actually found by the French UNPROFOR investigation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: First of all, we need to begin from the fact that there was no French investigation at the time when this statement about the Serb aggression was made. There was no investigation at all. There was just this angle of descent and some approximate line of direction leading to the front line, and that's all. That's when the statement was made. Only later when I started my own investigation did the French and others appear with some investigative efforts when it was all pointless, when it was all of it too little too late, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, let me say two things. First of all, I want to avoid semantic games with you and I want to remind you that Judge Robinson also pointed out your criticism of the particular term he used during his questioning of you in the Dragomir Milosevic case and defended his terminology. So I don't really want to get caught up in whether it was an investigation or a conclusion or preliminary efforts. Secondly, you seem to be suggesting here that there was nothing from the French until after your investigation was underway. And I want to remind you that during the course of the video, that is, the conference or the filming of your statement to the media, that you showed the -- a French document reflecting the number of mils for the line of direction; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I still insist that it was not a proper document. It was a piece of paper. It was not an investigation. An investigation means a thorough investigation of all possibilities, all leads. There was no -- there were no various options taken into account here. There was just this angle and one line of direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I -- I think everyone here understands that you take the position that further steps needed to be implemented before you would consider an investigation to be complete, but I'm just focusing now on the materials that you had at the time of the video that was made and that, in fact, you referred to as having relied upon because you consider them to be professional and honest efforts. So we're in agreement on that much; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that I took that into account. Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the moment I'm looking at the methodology that you used and just talk to you about the plus or minus aspect. Now I want to talk to you about where the figure 171 degrees came from. Now, Colonel, are you aware that the French did not find that the line of direction - as you stated in paragraph 122 of your amalgamated witness statement - was 171 degrees plus or minus 5?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what line of direction they found?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Of course I don't remember, but I remember that line that went left that was on the sketch, but I don't remember the figure. It doesn't matter anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest we will be looking at the distances represented by those different lines at some point, but let me focus on it at the moment in terms of methodology rather than overall consequences. So I take it then that -- and I can show you the document, for example, that shows that what the French found was 160 degrees line of direction. So I take it you don't dispute that? You're welcome to see the document if you wish.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, no, I believe it. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, 160 degrees in the French system is 2850 mils. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: (No verbal response)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you're nodding your head, yes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the Judges, although they may well be aware of this already, mils is a unit of angular measurement used in artillery in particular and that has quite a number depending on the particular system used; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Is it something you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the Russian system is it correct that 6.000 mils is the system used and a single mil is equal to 1/6000th of a revolution, or do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, there is a system of calculation in thousandth part and the system of calculation in degrees, one and the same system. It doesn't change anything. I'm not talking about millimetres. I'm talking about thousandth parts which is mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I just heard you say it's one and the same system, but are you not aware that the Russian system uses 6.000 mils for a complete revolution and the NATO countries use 6400 mils. Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just call up the simplest thing I can. We'll get more testimony on that, but if we could look at 65 ter 23896, just a Wikipedia article, something anybody can look up. We're also going to see some firing tables, I believe, that reflect the different system of mils. If we could just scroll down quickly. Okay. You can see in this first paragraph it indicates that France began with mils at 6400, the Red Army expanded that to 6.000 mil one. And if we continue with the article, we'll see that difference reflected again and confirmed. I don't want to get us too deeply into these sorts of details, as I say we'll see them further in the firing tables, but are you satisfied, Colonel, that there is a difference between the Russian system and the system that NATO countries use in terms of mils?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I don't mind that every country and every bloc has its own system of measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the reason I raise this is not for idle academic purposes, Colonel. This is the reason, that, as I say, the -- you have the translation of mils to degrees is obviously done by dividing the mils by 360 degrees and if you then get in the French system a figure of 17.777 for each mil, and if you divide 2850, which is the mils the French found, you get 160. So that's their figure of 160. And you can see in one of the documents in evidence that 2850 mils equals 160 degrees in the French system. However, Colonel, if you mistakenly use the mils that the French came up with, 2850, and then apply the Russian standard to that, that is, you divide 6.000 instead of 6400 by 360, you get a figure of 16.666 for each mil. And then if you divide 2850 mils, the figure reached by the French, with the Russian system of mils, you get the number 171 degrees. And isn't that, in fact, Colonel, how you came up with the figure 171 as reflected in your amalgamated witness statement at paragraph 122 because that 171 is reflected in no other finding by any other investigation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I object to that and I don't think that is correct to be put to the witness in that way, and perhaps if you want to hear more about that we could excuse the witness and I can explain, but there's a very misleading element to that statement that I think not fair to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why is the Prosecution not able to put something to the witness, which the witness, I'm confident, is able to deal with the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he's just made a statement of fact to the witness that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's leave it -- if Mr. Robinson is concerned with the last phrase I used, I can drop that, and I just want the witness's response about the actual data that was used and how he arrived at that figure. So I'll deal with the question of what other investigations came up with in a moment if that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry about that exchange. Do I need to repeat the question? Because the point is this: That by mixing and matching or by mixing up the two systems, that's how you come to the figure of 170 degrees. It's not the figure that was found by the French, it's not the figure that's represented by the -- that's reflected in the document you were showing the media on September 2nd when you held the conference?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Once again, this is my point of view. First of all, I agree with you, that this kind of conversion from our mils tables to the firing tables of NATO we did not do that, we didn't need to. The calculations were very simple and even more primitive than you suppose. I didn't even need to determine what 160 degrees was. We simply see the line drawn on the map - it doesn't matter at how many degrees - the line drawn by the French. And we see on the map what landmark on the ground this line reaches. We go to the ground, we go to those landmarks - there are ten on the road or whatever - and we investigate those points, those locations. We don't care how many degrees the French investigation reached; it doesn't matter. It is the old military principle of landmarks that has not been replaced by anything. There were no GPS systems then, at least we didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you talked to the media on September 2nd, you did not hold up a document that said here's the line on the map drawn by the French which I followed today. You held up a document that said: I know the angle of descent and I know the line -- from the Bosnian investigation and I know the line of direction from the French investigation. And that's what you represented your line of direction was based on; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: You know, 17 years ago it was difficult to imagine that we will be discussing this now, in legal terms, mind you, not military terms, not against the backdrop of shooting behind my back - and remember, there was a war going on then. I couldn't imagine that I would be in court 17 years later discussing in legal terms how we are to combine two different tables. I have to present briefly my arguments, what, why, and what needs to be done. At that time, of course, I wasn't thinking why I wasn't showing this or another document or the table, why didn't I comment on it? It's difficult to think 17 years ahead; just try it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you may well have done things a little bit different at the time if you knew you'd be in court 17 years ago, but I'm simply focusing on what you did at the time and what you said at the time. Let me turn to another issue that was raised in your amalgamated witness statement, and that is that assuming that you had followed the right line of direction, where you looked when you got to the spot that you considered the angle of descent and the number of charges indicated was a potential firing point. Now, there's a paragraph in your amalgamated witness statement devoted to the alleged confusion by the Trial Chamber between two margins of error. So let me turn first, since you impliedly refer to what the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber said, to what they did find about your conclusions and where you looked. And that's found at paragraph 722 of the Dragomir Milosevic judgement, and I think we can find that at 65 ter 23899 at page 7. It begins, and this is paragraph 722, after a discussion -- this follows a fairly lengthy discussion of the evidence you gave. It says that you testified about the mortar, went to the possible firing locations, concluded for each of the locations it was either not possible to fire or there were no visible traces. It goes on you could not testify as to exactly which bearing you used when you visited the possible firing locations. It talks about a satellite photograph that you were shown indicating the difference in the bearings, that you said the bearing was one from UNPROFOR. And then it goes on: "Colonel Demurenko testified he could calculate the possible firing locations with a margin of deviation of ten to 15 metres and that enabled him to search the location within those points. The Trial Chamber recalls the evidence that any bearing calculated by UNPROFOR or the Bosnia-Herzegovina police had a margin of error of approximately 10 degrees confirmed by QMS Higgs. It is clear that this margin of error covered a wider area than was covered by the locations visited by Colonel Demurenko on the basis of a margin of deviation of no more than 10 to 15 metres. The Trial Chamber therefore has a difficulty accepting Colonel Demurenko's conclusions, dismissing any possibility that the shell was fired from SRK-held territory. This determination is consistent with the Prosecution's line of cross-examination, that Colonel Demurenko confined himself to too narrow an area in seeking to identify the possible launching sights. It is significant that Colonel Demurenko never answered the Prosecution's questions on this point with any clarity. In fact, the Trial Chamber characterises his responses as vague and evasive." Now, that's what the Trial Chamber said. And in your amalgamated witness statement at paragraph 22, you stated that: "It seems that the Dragomir Milosevic confused these two margins of error ..." And by that you meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you give the para number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 122 I believe, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's noted as -- you said -- just 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show that paragraph to the witness as well. This is on page 55 end of that paragraph just before the next para. Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you scroll down slightly we will see at the end of that paragraph the quote I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, we could read the entirety of 122 along with paragraph 121, which is also relevant, but the two margins of error that you're referring to here are, one, the margin of error between -- margin of error for the difference between where a mortar is aimed and where it may actually land, that's on the one hand; and on the other hand, the deviation of error - I'll call it that - in assessing where a potential firing site was based on the firing tables, the number of charges, and the angle of descent. Correct? You're asserting that the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber confused those two?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, that's actually a statement to which I wish you to either affirm or deny. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything against the previous Chamber. I have full respect to this Court and I came here for the second time, so how could I doubt their conclusions or anything of the sort? I trust the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, if you -- I agree with you and if you're willing to rely on the findings of the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber and retract your testimony, we can end this cross-examination right now. But I understand you to be saying in paragraph 122 that the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber was confused about the two kinds of margins of error. So you tell me if I should proceed or not.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I don't understand what is your dilemma now. What are you actually asking me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we show the witness the previous page. So here in para 122 you first explained the table 1 we see here. And next page. And then you explain another set of a margin of error. And after that - no, further down - in the last sentence just below the table 2 you said: "It seems that the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber confused these two margin or errors (table 1 and table 2)." Could you clarify what you meant by this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask that the witness be given a hard copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. Do you have it with you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's on page 54 and 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There seem to be some documents inadvertently appended. I'll remove them and hand them back to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to tell you regarding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a feeling that if we are going to go into the depth of the artillery science, we won't get closer to the end - not only today but we won't get to it this year. Once it -- again, let me tell you, when the firing tables are prepared, there is a full set of facts and a partial one. So the deviation can depend not on two, like shown here, but dozens of tables. For example, in order to understand the deviation of a round, one needs not only to take the temperature of the charge but also the temperature of the lower level of the air where the shell landed and in the upper levels of air of the trajectory and additional dozens of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Let's make it simple. Do you see the sentence where you said: "It seems that Dragomir Milosevic Chamber confused these two margin or errors ..." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with the statement, that those two tables were absolutely not sufficient in order to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'll leave it to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, then I'll follow-up on the Trial Chamber's question. That was not the question. The question was simply whether or not you stand by the statement that they confused those two kinds of deviations or margins of error?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, I cannot blame somebody who made conclusions some time ago, five years ago. In order to do that, I would need to go into an in-depth study of their facts and conclusions and I'm not prepared to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, like you, Mr. President, I will leave it there for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you do not explain in your statement how it was, in your view, the Trial Chamber confused these two margins of error since there was no discussion during your testimony that I'm aware of about the margin of error representing the difference between where a mortar is aimed and where it lands, that that wasn't relevant to or addressed in your testimony at all. Isn't that right? That wasn't the subject of your testimony, you weren't asked about that, and the Trial Chamber wasn't interested in the -- how far a mortar may deviate from its intended target once fired?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I agree that we didn't discuss it in detail for a very clear reason. As I said in my initial statement and also when I testified in court, I have a very clear belief that there was no mortar shelling at all. This was a terrorist act carried out in the streets of Sarajevo. This is the first thing I wanted to say. The second thing is if I were to be given a sheet of paper or a screen where I could show you graphically the areas that we investigated, it would become clear to everybody that we not only explored the possible locations shown on the map; we explored the gigantic area, the entire slope of that mountain, thousands of square metres. And it was only after doing that that we concluded that no mortars could have been placed there because there was simply no location suitable for mortars to be put there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, I understand that's what you're saying now in the face of the Dragomir Milosevic testimony, but let's take a look then at what you said to the Chamber at the time about the nature of your examination to determine whether or not it was possible to have fired a mortar from the areas that you identified as potential firing spots. So first I'm going to run you through a number of things that you said to the Milosevic Chamber. First, at page -- transcript page 7780 you referred to specialists visiting location, marking the spot: " ... the very spot from which this shell was allegedly fired." And the same page you refer to: "I have on record photographs which show me pointing my finger on the location," that's 7780. At 7777 you said you and the others looked at firing tables in order to establish "with a margin of error of 1 to 2 metres the exact location ..." At 7781 you again refer to: " ... the exact locations of fire points ..." Again at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you for that admonition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again at 8992 you talk about pointing at a "precise" location, and indicate that: Each photograph was made in a particular location which "had been identified in advance with a margin of error of 5 metres." That's at 8992. And then again a bit later you stated that -- asked whether you could see any traces that a 120-millimetre mortar was placed in that area, and that is this exact location to which you had been referring, you said certainly: "And we observed the entire area around this spot, and had I seen 10 to 20 metres away from this spot a possible firing position" then that could have been something that would have prompted you to draw some other conclusions. So, Colonel, I put it to you that the Dragomir Milosevic Trial Chamber was not confused about the two different kinds of margins of error reflected in the tables you put into your amalgamated witness statement, but they understood you to be saying exactly what you were saying, that you were focused on very precise locations. That is the testimony you gave to the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Let me respond. That's right, because otherwise had I covered the map with my hand and said I investigated this entire area, it would not have sound convincing. One needs to be precise in the artillery sense precise and show everything that is open for calculation, that is, that can be calculated. So what we investigated were specific locations and I covered -- I spoke about all of them in quite precise terms because we had to show that we knew how to make calculations using the known angles in order to define the possible firing points. However, let me draw your attention to the fact that that doesn't exclude the possibility that not only 10 to 15 metres further, but 150 metres further and 200 metres further, everything was thoroughly investigated and photographed. And one doesn't contradict the other. Have I answered your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, but you have provided some additional information I want to follow-up on. So your suggestion is that this -- you -- as you said before, you went to all these areas but you were just showing the Trial Chamber how precise you -- your calculations were. And I put it to you, Colonel, that you had an opportunity in the Milosevic case to tell the Chamber that you covered all the terrain you now say you did because you -- the Trial Chamber confronted you about just this issue and asked about the precise nature of the locations you said you were focusing on. And you didn't tell them: No, no, no, no, it's true, it's -- it can't be -- you can't be that precise and I covered much more ground to make certain. Here's what you told them, Colonel, and let me describe to you the question that you were asked in the face of all this emphasis on precise locations that you made and then the answer that you gave. And this is at transcript 7705 through 06 in the Dragomir Milosevic testimony and indeed at paragraph 97 of your amalgamated witness statement. So

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "But Colonel, would there not be quite a large margin around each of these six firing points, and even so the farther out you get the larger the margin within which the fire could have been shot is increased. So if you take the example with the six charges, I mean, if it was fired from there, it could have been fired, I suppose, quite a large area. It did not necessarily have to be fired from the position where you were and where you took this photograph. If, for instance, a couple of hundred metres away there would have been a road or something else, the shot could have come from there. So are you able really to exclude that the mortar could not have been fired even from an area adjacent to the place where you were?" And your --

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I'm ready to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- you may be but I want to tell you the answer that you gave at the time. Because at that time you didn't say what you're saying today, that you covered a tremendous amount of ground. Here's what you said: "I have to emphasis one thing once again. I know this weapon very, very well. Maybe the interpretation of the word 'charge' was misleading. There are no different shells, six shells there. There are six charges. And it's charged manually. You put the shell inside the tube and it flies up. "So the firing tables for mortars that you saw in that video footage show that in that direction only six charges are possible, either one, two, three, all the six were taken into account." And then you said: "Margins of deviation are measured in metres, like 10 to 15 metres, the size of this room, but the margin of deviation cannot be a hundred metres. We took into account ballistic trajectories. It's the science of physics. We cannot go beyond that. If you take a certain line of fire, only six possible firing points exist depending on the charges used. We photographed an area of 20, 30 square metres. We always proceeded from a certain surface on which the mortar had to rely. It cannot hang in the air. It cannot be suspended on a tree. We showed the photographs and we saw the ground was pure and clear. No mortar had stood there." So with an opportunity to tell the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber, indeed not just an opportunity but an obligation because the Judge was asking you that very question, you didn't say that you went -- you covered the entire area for thousands and thousands of metres around. You said: Look, we looked at the precise spot and the 20 to 30 metres around it in order to determine that the mortar couldn't have been fired from there, and that's why the Milosevic Chamber reached the conclusion it did; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I'll answer that. Concerning the first part, at least I thought it was a question, it's necessary to answer the question about the road. Yes, in theory a road could be a relatively good place to place an artillery weapon. But in that place where we were there were -- there had never been any asphalt roads. There were just dirt tracks fit for horses. And on the ground, even on the dirt track like that, there would have been traces, traces of the base plate, traces of the cases of ammunition, and even if you tried to hide them to remove them, it would hardly be possible. That's as far as the road is concerned. The second thing: Why I didn't talk more about the area we covered. As a professional - not in geology but in another area of expertise - it's difficult for me to explain why I didn't speak about it. Perhaps they didn't ask me. They probably didn't ask me. But I have to say that in the interview on the video I said that we explored the locality. I didn't say a particular location or point. We explored the locality, and that means that we explored a large area lest we later be accused of a biased conclusion. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's be a little more concrete then because in fact you persist in saying that nobody -- let me see if I have that right. "They probably didn't ask me." Okay. Well, let's call up -- we've just -- I've just read to you in detail what Judge Harhoff indeed asked you and you were clearing talking about a meadow. So let's call up 1D08701. Now, in your testimony you referred to a pristine meadow, and this was -- I take it this is the meadow you were talking about because I can only recall one picture of a meadow among the four you showed in court.

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, this one included. But there was a huge number of photographs. We took loads of them, but yes this picture shows that my words are consistent with the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff clearly said you're pointing to an area that you looked at, but if there was a road adjacent maybe a couple of hundred of metres away, wouldn't that invalidate your conclusions? And you didn't say: No, it wouldn't because as you can see here there's a house and a road near it and I looked at that road. You said: I looked at the 20 to 30 square metres around the point that I identified as being the firing location. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would ask that Mr. Tieger read from the transcript as to exactly what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I read it just a few moments ago. Does Mr. Robinson really want to have that read again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just looking at paragraph 97 of the amalgamated statement which quotes from that portion, and I hesitate whether I should say this in the presence of the witness, but in any event, in the last -- second-to-last sentence it says that: " ... we photographed an area of 20 to 30 metres." It doesn't say we looked at an area of 20 to 30 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it also states, Mr. Demurenko, that the margin of deviation cannot be what the Judge said it was. You shouldn't worry about a road a couple of hundred metres away because margins of deviation are measured in metres like 10 to 15 metres, but the margin of deviation cannot be 100 metres. That's what you told the Milosevic Chamber; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: I'm not going to deny anything I said to a previous Chamber and I'm not going to deny anything I've said today. Everything I said I said perfectly sincerely and honestly. It's a different matter that somebody would like to catch me out in an inconsistency between what I said before and later. Perhaps there is such a strategy, but I repeat I am not a legal expert. I'm a soldier and everything I could say I've already said, and the rest is up to specialists in other areas of a different level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, in respect of leaving -- let's leave that aside for a different moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me try it for the last time. Why don't we show the last paragraph in para 122 of the witness's statement. You understand English, Mr. Demurenko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand it but I have misgivings because over the past few years I've had no practice. And if I can understand English in colloquial speech or perhaps enough to read a simpler book -- but in a serious discussion when every word - and not only every word but every full stop and comma is important - I would not rely on my English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page. And let's zoom in a bit. Could you kindly read two lines, one sentence, which appears immediately above paragraph 123. Could you read aloud. I will read it for your benefit so that you can hear the translation. "It seems that the Dragomir Milosevic Chamber confused these two margins or errors" and you refer to table 1 and table 2. This is your statement that you stated you would stand by. What did you mean by saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to recall my state of mind and level of understanding from five years ago. But in that specific case I meant that not all elements of artillery science were taken account. As I said 15 years ago there are not two tables that are relevant but 20 or 30, and it is not appropriate to compare one table with another and confine yourself to that. We should either limit ourselves to a margin of several centimetres or take into account properly all the 30 tables that are relevant. That's I think what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But this is the statement you made recently, not five years ago. So could you clarify that, what you meant. Why did you -- do you think the Milosevic Chamber was confused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult for me to judge the basis on which this high court made its conclusions. I believe it was done the way it was done simply because we should not look at the accessories on a suit, on an outfit, but the whole suit, the main thing, not second-rate or third-rate details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it help, Your Excellency, if the witness had read out to him paragraphs 122 and 123 so they be interpreted into Russian so that he should realise it refers to the judgement in the Dragomir Milosevic case. If we could read to him both these paragraphs, 122 and 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger did it, but it may be a subject for you to take up at your re-examination if necessary. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. In the remaining time before I move on to an entirely different area, let me just address this. Let me just focus on your assertion that you were looking for various traces that a mortar had been fired. First of all, can we agree that there is likely to be a difference between the traces of a fixed mortar position that has been in a particular place for a period of time and the traces left by a mortar that assumes a temporary firing position for one shot and then departs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. Firing positions that have been occupied for years certainly leave more traces or deeper traces. But nevertheless, even a temporarily-placed mortar would inevitably leave a trace, especially if it has been fired. If it has been just placed there without firing and then evacuated somehow by a crane, there would be minimal trace. But if it has been fired, the crew would never be able to remove all the traces of the gun charge that has been fired but does not depart with the shell. But the main argument for all artillery specialists is that there is one in a million chance that one single mortar would manage to hit one single street occupied by a huge crowd of people. And let me remind you that two years earlier there had been an identical terrorist act in the same street, killing 88 people and wounding 200. The chance that a mortar shell would hit such a small street of 6, 8 metres in length distance between those two buildings is one in a million. It's virtually impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is the chance slightly higher that a mortar will land in a broader area rather than the precise spot on which it lands? And are you asserting here that your judgement about whether -- about where the mortar was fired from and whether it was a mortar at all is based on your conclusion that that exact spot, right there, was the target rather than, for example, the market at large?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, Mr. Tieger is putting multiple questions to the witness which is something that he criticised Dr. Karadzic for. So I think if he can break it up and just take an answer to his first question then he can follow it up with the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'll ask the question. Are you asserting here that your conclusions are based upon your insistence that the mortar was fired at the exact spot it landed -- that the mortar was targeted at the exact spot it landed rather than, for example, the market at large?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, no. That is not so. Moreover, I insist that there was no mortar fire. That's what I insist on. But even if we accept for the moment the fantastic idea that one mortar was firing at the city with minimal chances of hitting a very small, densely populated area, I'm saying the chance is one in a million. I want to remind this honourable Court and everybody that on that day it was not the one explosion registered by UN representatives. I believe there were six detonations, six explosions in that area. And after the first five mortar shells or so-called mortar shells, only five people were wounded. And from this particular shell allegedly killed 88 and wounded 200. That doesn't happen. It just doesn't happen that a shell chooses on its own a point where it would do the most damage and the greatest casualties. There were so many details of that kind presented in the statement made to the public and the image created that just doesn't -- don't hold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I understand you to be saying that you scoured thousands of metres of territory in order to look for the traces of a mortar shell that you believed had not been fired?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you went out there, you say, thinking that you would -- that there was nothing to be found; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: No, no. I wanted to either confirm what the speaker -- what the spokesman said - that it was from Serb territory - I wanted to confirm it if I was able to by photographs and finding traces, but in the end my inquiry, my investigation, showed it to be a lie. The objective was reached. My objective was not to refute it. My objective was to find the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you consider that you might be allegedly looking for the trace of a mortar that was fired from a temporary position, that is, which someone had just driven up, taken the mortar off in about a minute or two, fired it maybe from sandbags, and then departed? Did you consider that possibility and is that what you say you were looking for in-depth?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: We were looking for any object, any clue, any lead that would indicate an unnatural change in the area. Sand would seep to the ground from those sandbags. Nobody travelled there with sandbags anyway. There would be some trace of the charge, there would be fragments from the shells. We were looking for anything that would stand out and anything we found could be in support of the UN theory. But we didn't find anything like that. And I believe what we found was true, you have to -- I have to remind you, the slope is very steep, 70 degrees or so. Nobody fired from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 70 degrees, just enough to clear the building and land right in the street?

utterances.speaker: ANDREY DEMURENKO
utterances.text: Yes, it is a hypocritical way of looking at it. If the shell had flown over the roofs, it would be just a few centimetres over the roofs. And in massive artillery attacks, that's what happens. The shells land in the street over the roofs, but that's in massive artillery attacks, using just one shot from a mortar the chances are one in a million that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We're obviously done for the day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will continue tomorrow, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn soon, but, Mr. Demurenko, can I remind you that you're not supposed to discuss about your testimony with anybody else, including the parties, Defence, and Prosecution. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of October, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.45 p.m.,
